title: The age of the genius general is over
gist: A retired RAF air marshal argues the British military's institutional cult of the intuitive 'genius general' — symbolised by the kingfisher badge of the Higher Command and Staff Course and reinforced by Churchill and Alanbrooke — selects for cuffers, bluffers and chancers through rigid first-look promotion windows, and will be actively regressive in an era of AI, data-at-the-edge and autonomous systems. He draws the explicit parallel to finance: Taleb's evidence that hedge funds underperform random decisions, and the fact that quants and fibre-optic latency, not Wolfe's 'Masters of the Universe', made the money — with Ukraine (defence budget one-twelfth of the UK's) proving what cheap dual-use tech like Starlink, Palantir and civilian drones can do.

themes.theme: The Genius-General Myth as Institutional Design

insights.claim: The kingfisher is the emblem of the British Higher Command and Staff Course at the Defence Academy at Shrivenham, chosen for T.E. Lawrence's claim that nine-tenths of tactics are teachable but the 'irrational tenth' is the test of generals — encoding unteachable intuition as the institution's official theory of leadership.
insights.speaker: Edward Stringer
insights.so_what: When an institution's selection symbol asserts the key skill is untestable, the selection process cannot be audited — a structural governance failure worth recognising in any promotion system.
insights.quote: Nine-tenths of tactics are certain, and taught in books, but the irrational tenth is like the kingfisher flashing across the pool, and that is the test of generals.
insights.locator: Myths and symbols persist

insights.claim: Churchill, writing his biography of Marlborough just before the Second World War, held that nothing but genius — 'the daemon in man' — can answer the riddles of war and that genius cannot be acquired by reading or experience, a doctrine the author says still shapes what British generals are taught to emulate.
insights.speaker: Edward Stringer
insights.so_what: The intellectual root of the problem is a canonical text still taught — meaning reform requires changing the curriculum, not just the incentives.
insights.quote: Nothing but genius, the daemon in man, can answer the riddles of war, and genius, though it may be armed, cannot be acquired, either by reading or by experience.
insights.locator: Churchill wrote that

insights.claim: Advancement in the higher echelons of the British military hinges on convincing superiors you have an undefined and unmeasurable quality called 'it', while the assessing general never has to justify that judgement either — which is why senior military leadership tends to follow tribal cycles.
insights.speaker: Edward Stringer
insights.so_what: Unfalsifiable, mutually unaccountable assessment reproduces the incumbent type indefinitely — the clearest diagnostic of a self-sealing elite.
insights.locator: ‘Getting on’ in the higher echelons

insights.claim: Alanbrooke's wartime diaries, still treated as a bible by the modern ambitious general, reinforce the charismatic genius-general trope despite their frustration with Churchill.
insights.speaker: Edward Stringer
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific texts transmitting the culture — the practical target for anyone trying to change officer formation.
insights.locator: Add in Field Marshal Lord Alanbrooke

insights.claim: The British promotion hierarchy only allows promotion of cohorts leaving Sandhurst within a set window, so 'first look promotees' get the best 'black bag' jobs, the strongest performance report tariffs and pole position at the next window — making it all but impossible for late developers, the unlucky, or those who won't game the system to catch up.
insights.speaker: Edward Stringer
insights.so_what: A compounding-advantage tournament decided very early — the mechanism by which one selection error propagates to the top of an organisation.
insights.locator: And so will fight with belief.

insights.claim: Sandhurst's mantra that the only thing worse than a bad plan is no plan at all, combined with doctrine's emphasis on tempo and offensive action, produces a culture where whoever darts in first with something plausible wins — appropriate for a junior officer facing simple problems but not for wicked strategic ones.
insights.speaker: Edward Stringer
insights.so_what: Traits optimal at one organisational altitude become liabilities at another — the general failure mode of promoting on early-career signal.
insights.quote: you have a culture where he who darts in first with something plausible wins
insights.locator: Every officer cadet arriving at the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst

insights.claim: The cohort that reaches senior strategic rank in the British military is likely to be composed of those who can throw something together off the cuff, style it out, and seize the moment with elbows sharpened — streetwise attributes that do not necessarily produce an Eisenhower.
insights.speaker: Edward Stringer
insights.so_what: Names the actual selected phenotype versus the advertised one — the gap between an institution's stated and revealed talent preference.
insights.quote: This cohort is likely to include those who can throw something together off the cuff (cuffers), those who can style it out (bluffers) and those who seize the moment with elbows sharpened (chancers).
insights.locator: So we now have the first step to make senior, strategic rank.

insights.claim: Selection for the Higher Command and Staff Course is such a bottleneck for higher rank that failure to be selected is a make-or-break moment prompting some officers to leave their service outright.
insights.speaker: Edward Stringer
insights.so_what: A single chokepoint gate means talent loss is concentrated at one decision — high leverage for reform and high fragility to bias.
insights.locator: The next pivotal selection within the British military

insights.claim: Churchill repeatedly tried to remove several of the Second World War's most competent commanders — including Tedder in the Mediterranean and Slim in Burma — largely for offering realistic assessments of dire situations rather than being swashbuckling, while tolerating late-era Montgomery's ego and favouring Harold Alexander on appearance and bearing regardless of results.
insights.speaker: Edward Stringer
insights.so_what: Direct historical evidence that charisma-weighted selection systematically mispriced talent — the best available proof the current heuristic fails.
insights.locator: The general point I shall hurry over.

insights.claim: The Confederacy is widely considered to have had the best battlefield commanders of the American Civil War in Jackson, Longstreet and Stuart and still lost, because war was decided by finances and modern methods of production and communication — demonstrating that war and warfare are not the same thing.
insights.speaker: Edward Stringer
insights.so_what: Tactical excellence cannot offset structural economic and industrial disadvantage — the same logic applies to any conflict assessment weighted toward battlefield performance.
insights.locator: The macro-observation is that the Southern states

insights.claim: Ulysses S. Grant had left the army after an unremarkable career largely in the back-room divisions of supply and administration, and had always lost out to 'bustling, bonhomious, chance-grabbing optimists' — but the very logistics capacities he specialised in were being rewritten by civilian-led advances, and officers with railway and telegraph expertise were rapidly promoted to senior rank.
insights.speaker: Edward Stringer
insights.so_what: The historical template for the article's central bet: when the technology base of war changes, back-office specialists become the decisive commanders — apply it to who gets promoted in the AI transition.
insights.locator: The linking figure that brings us back

insights.claim: Soviet generals used to scoff that every German the British came up against was 'a genius' while they had no trouble beating them all, and the author sees evidence of this 'Rommel Effect' in the behaviour of some British generals of the Second World War.
insights.speaker: Edward Stringer
insights.so_what: Inflating the adversary's genius is an excuse-generating mechanism — worth watching wherever an institution explains failure by the opponent's brilliance.
insights.quote: every German the British came up against was ‘a genius’, while they had no trouble beating them all
insights.locator: Soviet generals used to scoff

insights.claim: Ukraine, with a peacetime defence budget one-twelfth that of the UK and less than 1 percent that of the USA, reimagined modern warfare by repurposing largely civilian dual-use technologies — SpaceX's Starlink, Palantir's data-analysis tools and myriad civilian drones — integrated via the cloud into a slick advanced command and control system.
insights.speaker: Edward Stringer
insights.so_what: The clearest empirical case that dual-use commercial tech delivers military capability at a fraction of legacy platform cost — the core argument behind defence-tech reallocation.
insights.locator: Ukraine has revealed what a country

insights.claim: Ukraine achieved this rebuild not from an already advanced Western baseline but from a recent post-Soviet one, which the author calls a stunning achievement and evidence that organisational imagination, not starting technology level, is the binding constraint.
insights.speaker: Edward Stringer
insights.so_what: Removes the excuse that legacy modernisation is the prerequisite — organisational change can outrun capital stock.
insights.locator: Remarkably, the Ukrainians have rebuilt

insights.claim: Ukraine has achieved only a fraction of what is theoretically possible if the combinations of AI, data-at-the-edge and autonomous systems were unleashed with a NATO-scale budget.
insights.speaker: Edward Stringer
insights.so_what: Frames current battlefield tech as early-stage relative to the funded ceiling — a long runway for edge-compute, autonomy and military AI integration spend.
insights.locator: Even so, they have achieved but a fraction

insights.claim: Future military networks will be flatter, faster and less hierarchical, requiring cooperation across traditional command boundaries that are framed hierarchically and geographically — making understanding how these networks function in practice a vital command skill in its own right.
insights.speaker: Edward Stringer
insights.so_what: A new, teachable and testable competency replaces intuition as the selection criterion — the practical reform implied by the whole essay.
insights.locator: The networks are flatter and faster

insights.claim: AI will chew over orders of magnitude more data than any previous 'mandraulic' system could assimilate, its algorithms self-trained to the point of being beyond the initial programmer's understanding, and will generate counterintuitive analysis and options — leaving open the question of how a system predicated on a single genius general's intuition can cope.
insights.speaker: Edward Stringer
insights.so_what: The tension between opaque machine recommendations and intuition-based authority is the governance problem that will determine whether military AI adoption actually delivers.
insights.locator: But as we move into the Information Age

themes.theme: Finance Parallel: Quants vs Masters of the Universe

insights.claim: Citing Taleb's Fooled by Randomness, the author notes that analysing the performance of multiple hedge funds over time produces slightly fewer successes than would occur if decisions were taken at random, yet we construct backward narratives explaining why particular financial geniuses succeeded so we may follow them.
insights.speaker: Edward Stringer
insights.so_what: The manager-skill illusion and the genius-general illusion are the same cognitive error — a direct warning against paying for narrative rather than process.
insights.locator: The febrile world of finance provides intriguing parallels

insights.claim: For a time the trading edge lay in understanding data latency in fibre-optic transmission of laser pulses, so physical geography mattered more than the intuitive genius of the guru, and it is the mathematical and computational quants who made companies fortunes while Wolfe's 'Masters of the Universe' remained the public front.
insights.speaker: Edward Stringer
insights.so_what: The visible star and the actual source of returns diverge — a check on attributing performance to the person fronting a strategy.
insights.locator: In reality, much trading is now driven at frantic speed by algorithms.

insights.claim: The author raises the open question of whether stock market success depends on the fundamentals of business and economics or on understanding and perhaps manipulating the herd mentality of investors — because if it is the latter, cultivating a persona of confident invulnerability is rational since your own words and deeds may shape the market to profitable effect.
insights.speaker: Edward Stringer
insights.so_what: If reflexivity dominates, then charisma is not noise but part of the return-generating mechanism — which complicates the whole 'promote the quants' prescription.
insights.locator: There is another argument to be explored here

insights.claim: Whole industries were created around emulating the 'Masters of the Universe', and these are only slightly dented when a Master falls spectacularly, because our longing for compelling narratives and heroic explanations of success is atavistic.
insights.speaker: Edward Stringer
insights.so_what: Narrative demand survives falsification, so mispricing of star operators is persistent rather than self-correcting.
insights.locator: Whole industries are created around emulating

insights.claim: Fetishising generalship as an innate product of genius creates a version of moral hazard: officers wanting to demonstrate those qualities may be encouraged to gamble, overreach and cover up until they can make good, and once at general rank can inhale their own smoke and believe they need not justify decisions that are little more than whimsy.
insights.speaker: Edward Stringer
insights.so_what: The named transmission path from culture to concealed failure — the same pathology that produces hidden risk in trading desks and unaccountable executives.
insights.locator: The danger is that if we fetishise the idea

insights.claim: The heroic school of leadership produces superheated command systems where competitive personalities and egos dominate, and in peacetime such manoeuvring is useful in Whitehall funding battles — giving the culture an ongoing institutional payoff independent of battlefield merit.
insights.speaker: Edward Stringer
insights.so_what: Budget politics actively rewards the dysfunction, explaining why it is self-sustaining and hard to reform.
insights.locator: In peacetime, of course, such manoeuvrings can be useful

insights.claim: The author's prescription is to approach the AI-era command question with open-minded inquiry rather than an instinctive sense of the answer, being 'like savvy bank bosses who can see that the nerds might make better bets', and to revisit current teachings on command and generalship.
insights.speaker: Edward Stringer
insights.so_what: An explicit cross-domain instruction: the institutions that let the quantitative specialists run the book outperform those that keep the charismatic front in charge.
insights.quote: We need to be like savvy bank bosses who can see that the nerds might make better bets.
insights.locator: The answer is we don’t know.

insights.claim: Those whose success was built on an intuitive sense of how to game the previous era's incentives are the least likely to be able to adapt to the counterintuitive possibilities of tomorrow, and in an epoch where a general's intuition may be trumped by a man-machine team, these traits become actively regressive.
insights.speaker: Edward Stringer
insights.so_what: A general rule for any incumbent leadership cohort facing a technology regime change — prior-era optimisation is negatively predictive of next-era performance.
insights.quote: Those whose success was built on an intuitive sense of how to game the previous era’s incentives are the least likely to be able to adapt to the counterintuitive possibilities of tomorrow.
insights.locator: In short, it is time to revisit the fetishes
